q-146348.name: Question 1
q-146348.problem:
Suppose we have a population of size $N=75,$ where $80%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the population has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1,…,75.$ Find $P({X}_{2}=0|{X}_{1}=0).$
q-146348.worked_solution:
We have a population of size $N=75,$ and $p=0.8$ represents the proportion of the population with the characteristic. 

Therefore,

- the number of population members *with* the characteristic equals 

$$
Np=75(0.8)=60,
$$

- the number of population members *without* the characteristic equals 

$$
N(1-p)=75(1-0.8)=15.
$$

We select two members of the population at random. We need to find $P({X}_{2}=0|{X}_{1}=0),$ the probability that the second member does not have the characteristic given that the first member does not have the characteristic either.

If the first member does not have the characteristic, we have

$\,$ $N-1=75-1=74$ members remaining, and

$\,$ $N(1-p)-1=14$ members remaining who do not have the characteristic.

Therefore,

$$
P({X}_{2}=0|{X}_{1}=0)=\frac{N(1-p)-1}{N-1}=\frac{14}{74}=\frac{7}{37}.
$$

q-146399.name: Question 6
q-146399.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=130$ from a population where $35%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,130.$ Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic $X={\sum }_{i=1}^{130}{X}_{i}.$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146399.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p).$ 

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=35%=0.35,\,n=130.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(130,0.35).
$$

$$

q-146402.worked_solution:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=48%=0.48,\,n=180.
$$

$$
X≈B(180,0.48).

q-146303.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=20$ from a population where $55%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,20.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{20}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146303.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=55%=0.55,\,n=20.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(20,0.55)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =20\cdot 0.55 \\  & =11 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =20\cdot 0.55\cdot (1-0.55) \\  & =4.95\end{aligned}
$$

q-146404.name: Question 9
q-146404.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=45$ from a population where $20%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,45.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{45}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146404.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=20%=0.2,\,n=45.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(45,0.2)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =45\cdot 0.2 \\  & =9 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =45\cdot 0.2\cdot (1-0.2) \\  & =7.2\end{aligned}
$$

q-146407.name: Question 10
q-146407.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=400$ from a population where $32%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,400.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{400}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146407.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=32%=0.32,\,n=400.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(400,0.32)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =400\cdot 0.32 \\  & =128 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =400\cdot 0.32\cdot (1-0.32) \\  & =87.04\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size n=400 from a population where 32% of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable Xi be equal to Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise where i=1,…,400. If the statistic X is defined as X=∑i=1400Xi find approximate values of E[X] and Var[X].

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[X]=121,Var[X]=81.33
b
E[X]=128,Var[X]=81.27
c
E[X]=121,Var[X]=75.66
d
E[X]=128,Var[X]=87.04
e
E[X]=128,Var[X]=93.56
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise

Now, provided that N≫n, the random variables Xi can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have Xi∼Bernoulli(p)1≤i≤n where p is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable X, defined as X=∑i=1nXi can be approximated as a binomial random variable X≈B(n,p), where E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have p=32%=0.32,n=400.

Therefore, X≈B(400,0.32) and we have the following results for the mean and variance: E[X]=np=400⋅0.32=128Var[X]=np(1−p)=400⋅0.32⋅(1−0.32)=87.04

q-146295.name: Question 11
q-146295.problem:
Suppose that $45%$ of the voting population plans to vote for candidate $A$ in the upcoming mayoral election. A random sample of size $n=20$ is taken from the population and asked about their voting preference. 

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of voters in the sample that plan to vote for candidate $A?$ Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146295.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=45%=0.45,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =45%=0.45, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.45(1-0.45)}{20} \\  & ≈0.0124\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

q-146450.name: Question 12
q-146450.problem:
Suppose that  $8%$ of a particular university's student population attends the law school. A random sample of $n=100$ students is taken from the population and asked which school they attend.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who attend the law school? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146450.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=8%=0.08,$ and $n=100.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =8%=0.08, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.08(1-0.08)}{100} \\  & ≈0.0007\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

q-146447.name: Question 13
q-146447.problem:
Suppose that $22%$ of a particular population of teenagers like science fiction novels. A random sample of $n=25$ teenagers is taken from the population and asked about their favorite novel genres.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of teenagers in the sample who like science fiction novels? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
q-146447.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=22%=0.22,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =22%=0.22, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.22(1-0.22)}{25} \\  & ≈0.0069\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

q-146449.name: Question 14
q-146449.problem:
In a sports warehouse, a large container contains several thousand baseballs. According to a report from the manufacturer, $10%$ of these balls are defective. 

A random sample of size $n=20$ is taken from the container. What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of defective balls in the sample?

*Hint: You may assume that the number of baseballs in the box is significantly larger than the number in the sample.*
q-146449.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=10%=0.1,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =10%=0.1, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.1(1-0.1)}{20} \\  & =0.0045.\end{aligned}
$$

q-146441.name: Question 15
q-146441.problem:
A bag contains a large number of equally-sized buttons, of which $15%$ are white. A random sample of $n=18$ buttons is taken from the bag.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of white buttons in the sample? Round your answers to $3$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the number of buttons in the bag is significantly larger than the number in the sample.*
q-146441.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=15%=0.15,$ and $n=18.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =15%=0.15, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.15(1-0.15)}{18} \\  & ≈0.007\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Question 15

A bag contains a large number of equally-sized buttons, of which 15% are white. A random sample of n=18 buttons is taken from the bag.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of white buttons in the sample? Round your answers to 3 decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the number of buttons in the bag is significantly larger than the number in the sample.

a
E[p^]=0.15,Var[p^]=0.012
b
E[p^]=0.85,Var[p^]=0.007
c
E[p^]=0.15,Var[p^]=0.005
d
E[p^]=0.15,Var[p^]=0.007
e
E[p^]=0.85,Var[p^]=0.012
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=15%=0.15, and n=18. Therefore, E[p^]=15%=0.15,Var[p^]=0.15(1−0.15)18≈0.007 rounded to 3 decimal places.
